bamo-bamo8-2022-a.title: Greedy: make each next digit as large as possible
bamo-bamo8-2022-a.body:
Every arrangement gives a number with the same number of digits ($9\cdot1+90\cdot2+3=192$). For numbers of the same length, the larger one is the one with the larger digit at the first place where they differ, as in alphabetical order. So we choose cards from left to right, each time making the next digits as large as possible.

**Leading digit.** All cards starting with $9$ come first, then all starting with $8$, and so on down to $1$. (The card $100$ starts with $1$.)

**Order within a block.** Two cards $X$ and $Y$ should be placed as $XY$ rather than $YX$ when the string $XY$ is larger than $YX$. Within the block of cards starting with $d$:
- the two-digit cards go in decreasing order: $d9, d8, \dots, d0$;
- the one-digit card $d$ goes after $d(d+1)$ and before $d(d-1)$. For example $787>778$, so $78$ goes before $7$, and $776>767$, so $7$ goes before $76$;
- $d$ and $dd$ give the same string in either order ($777$).

So the block for digit $d$ is $d9,d8,\dots,d(d{+}1),\ d,\ dd,\ d(d{-}1),\dots,d0$ (with $d$ and $dd$ interchangeable). For $d=9$ the block is just $9,99,98,\dots,90$. For $d=1$ we must also place $100$. It belongs after every other card starting with $1$ (for example $10\,100>100\,10$ and $11\,100>100\,11$), so it goes last.

**Answer:**
$$9\ 99\ 98\cdots90\ \ 89\ 8\ 88\ 87\cdots80\ \ 79\ 78\ 7\ 77\ 76\cdots70\ \ \cdots\ \ 19\ 18\cdots12\ 1\ 11\ 10\ 100,$$
where each pair $d,\ dd$ may be swapped.

bamo-bamo8-2022-a.title: Sorting rule check
bamo-bamo8-2022-a.body:
A neat way to state the rule: put card $X$ before card $Y$ whenever the string $XY$ is larger than the string $YX$. This rule is consistent (it orders the cards like comparing their infinite repetitions $XXX\ldots$), and sorting by it gives the largest concatenation. If two neighbouring cards were in the wrong order, swapping them would increase the number. Sorting the cards $1,\dots,100$ by this rule gives exactly
$$9,99,98,\dots,90,89,8,88,87,\dots,80,79,78,7,77,\dots,23,2,22,21,\dots,12,1,11,10,100.$$

bamo-bamo8-2022-b.title: Solve for the percentage
bamo-bamo8-2022-b.body:
Let the percentage be $r$ written as a decimal (for $20\%$, $r=0.2$), and let $p$ be the agreed price. Then
$$p=a(1+r)=b(1-r).$$
From $a+ar=b-br$ we get $(a+b)r=b-a$, so $r=\dfrac{b-a}{a+b}$. Therefore
$$p=a\left(1+\frac{b-a}{a+b}\right)=a\cdot\frac{(a+b)+(b-a)}{a+b}=\frac{2ab}{a+b}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}$ dollars** (the *harmonic mean* of $a$ and $b$).

bamo-bamo8-2022-b.title: Use reciprocals
bamo-bamo8-2022-b.body:
From $p=a(1+r)$ and $p=b(1-r)$:
$$\frac pa=1+r,\qquad \frac pb=1-r.$$
Adding eliminates $r$: $\dfrac pa+\dfrac pb=2$, so $p\left(\dfrac{a+b}{ab}\right)=2$ and $p=\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}$.

(Check: $a=60$, $b=100$ gives $p=75$; that is $60$ raised by $25\%$, and $100$ lowered by $25\%$.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}$**

bamo-bamo8-2022-c.title: Pigeonhole with six regions
Outer ring and inner triangle
bamo-bamo8-2022-c.body:
Suppose no two striped balls touch. The $3$ inner balls $(3,2),(4,2),(4,3)$ all touch each other, so at most one of them is striped. The $12$ outer balls form a closed ring in which consecutive balls touch, so at most $6$ of them can be striped, and exactly $6$ only if striped and solid balls alternate around the ring. Since $7$ balls are striped, exactly $6$ outer and $1$ inner ball are striped, and the outer ones alternate.

Each inner ball touches two outer balls that are neighbours in the ring: $(3,2)$ touches $(2,2),(3,3)$; $(4,2)$ touches $(3,1),(4,1)$; $(4,3)$ touches $(3,3),(4,4)$. In an alternating ring, one of any two neighbours is striped. So the striped inner ball touches a striped outer ball, a contradiction. ∎

bamo-bamo8-2022-d.title: Remainders in an arithmetic progression
bamo-bamo8-2022-d.body:
**Lemma.** Let $q$ be a prime with $q\nmid d$. Then any $q$ consecutive terms $a, a+d,\dots,a+(q-1)d$ leave $q$ different remainders mod $q$, so exactly one of them is divisible by $q$.

*Proof.* If $a+id$ and $a+jd$ ($0\le i<j\le q-1$) had the same remainder, then $q\mid (j-i)d$. Since $q$ is prime, $q\mid j-i$ or $q\mid d$. But $0<j-i<q$ and $q\nmid d$. So the $q$ remainders are different, and they must be all of $0,1,\dots,q-1$. $\square$

The six terms are distinct, since $d>0$.

- **$2\mid d$.** If $d$ is odd, the terms alternate between even and odd, so three of them are even. At most one of them equals $2$, so another even term is larger than $2$ and not prime.
- **$3\mid d$.** If not, the lemma gives a multiple of $3$ among $p,p+d,p+2d$ and another among $p+3d,p+4d,p+5d$. At most one of them equals $3$, so the other is a multiple of $3$ larger than $3$, not prime.
- **$5\mid d$.** We now know $6\mid d$, so $d\ge 6$. If $5\nmid d$, the lemma gives a multiple of $5$ among $p+d,\dots,p+5d$. All of these are at least $2+6=8>5$, so it is not prime.

So $2$, $3$, and $5$ all divide $d$ (so $30\mid d$; e.g. $7,37,67,97,127,157$ works). ∎

bamo-bamo8-2022-e.title: Use a longest side
bamo-bamo8-2022-e.body:
Let $PQ$ be a side of maximal length $L$. Choose coordinates with $P=(0,0)$ and $Q=(L,0)$. For a point $V=(x,y)$, the perpendicular from $V$ to line $PQ$ meets the segment $PQ$ exactly when $0\le x\le L$. We must find a vertex other than $P,Q$ with $0\le x\le L$.

Suppose there is none. Walk around the polygon from $Q$ to $P$ the long way (not along side $PQ$): $Q=V_1,V_2,\dots,V_m=P$ with $m\ge3$. Every intermediate vertex $V_2,\dots,V_{m-1}$ has $x<0$ or $x>L$. Let $i$ be the last index with $x(V_i)\ge L$ (it exists since $x(V_1)=L$). Then $i<m$, and $V_{i+1}$ has $x\le 0$: either $V_{i+1}=P$, or it is an intermediate vertex with $x<L$, hence $x<0$.

The side $V_iV_{i+1}$ has length at least its horizontal extent $x(V_i)-x(V_{i+1})\ge L$. Equality would need $x(V_i)=L$ and $x(V_{i+1})=0$, i.e. $V_i=Q$ and $V_{i+1}=P$. That is impossible: $V_{i+1}=V_2\ne P$ when $i=1$, because $m\ge3$. So the side $V_iV_{i+1}$ is longer than $L$, which contradicts the choice of $PQ$.

Hence some vertex $A\ne P,Q$ has $0\le x(A)\le L$, and the perpendicular from $A$ to line $PQ$ meets the segment $PQ$. ∎

bamo-bamo12-2022-4.title: Integer and fractional parts
bamo-bamo12-2022-4.body:
Put the wire on $[0,10)$ (landing exactly at $10$ has probability $0$). Write each position as $x=\lfloor x\rfloor+\{x\}$ with integer part $\lfloor x\rfloor\in\{0,\dots,9\}$ and fractional part $\{x\}\in[0,1)$. Choosing $x$ uniformly is the same as choosing $\lfloor x\rfloor$ uniformly from $\{0,\dots,9\}$ and, independently, $\{x\}$ uniformly from $[0,1)$. With probability $1$ all ten fractional parts are different, so assume this.

- If two birds have the same integer part, they are less than $1$ apart. So the birds must have the **ten different integer parts** $0,1,\dots,9$, one each.
- Then bird $i$ (the one with integer part $i$) and bird $i-1$ are neighbours, at distance $1+\{x_i\}-\{x_{i-1}\}$. This is more than $1$ exactly when $\{x_i\}>\{x_{i-1}\}$.

So the birds are far enough apart **exactly when the order of the integer parts agrees with the order of the fractional parts**. Now condition on the ten fractional parts. They determine an ordering of the birds, $b_0,b_1,\dots,b_9$ by increasing fractional part, and the event says bird $b_i$ has integer part $i$ for every $i$. The integer parts are independent of the fractional parts and of each other, each uniform on $10$ values. So this happens with probability $\left(\tfrac1{10}\right)^{10}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{1}{10^{10}}$**

bamo-bamo12-2022-4.title: Squeeze out the gaps
bamo-bamo12-2022-4.body:
Order the birds' positions $y_1<y_2<\dots<y_{10}$. The condition is $y_{j+1}-y_j>1$ for all $j$. Map such a configuration to $z_j=y_j-(j-1)$. Then $0\le z_1<z_2<\dots<z_{10}<10-9=1$. Conversely, any increasing $z_1<\dots<z_{10}$ in $[0,1)$ gives a valid configuration via $y_j=z_j+(j-1)$. This shift preserves volume. So the set of good ordered configurations has the same volume as the set $\{0\le z_1<\dots<z_{10}<1\}$, which is $\tfrac{1}{10!}$. All ordered configurations $0\le y_1<\dots<y_{10}<10$ have volume $\tfrac{10^{10}}{10!}$. The probability is
$$\frac{1/10!}{10^{10}/10!}=\frac1{10^{10}}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{1}{10^{10}}$**

bamo-bamo12-2022-5.title: Case analysis with binary searches
bamo-bamo12-2022-5.body:
**Setup.** Write $f(x)=(x-r_1)(x-r_2)(x-r_3)$ (the leading coefficient is $1$). The $x^2$ coefficient is $-(r_1+r_2+r_3)=0$, so **the roots sum to $0$**, and knowing the roots determines $f$.

**Binary search lemma.** Suppose an unknown integer $r$ is one of $M\ge1$ known consecutive candidates, and a query at an integer $m$ tells us whether $r<m$, $r=m$, or $r>m$. Then $\lfloor\log_2 M\rfloor$ queries suffice. (Ask at the $(\lfloor M/2\rfloor+1)$-th candidate. Either we hit $r$, or at most $\lfloor M/2\rfloor$ candidates remain. Induct, with $0$ queries needed when $M=1$.)

**First move: ask the sign of $f(0)=-r_1r_2r_3$.**

**Case 1: $f(0)=0$.** Then the roots are $-r,0,r$ with $0\le r\le N-1$, and $f(x)=x(x-r)(x+r)$. For $x>0$, the sign of $f(x)$ is the sign of $x-r$, so a query at a positive integer $m$ compares $r$ with $m$. There are $N=3\cdot2^k$ candidates, so by the lemma $\lfloor\log_2(3\cdot2^k)\rfloor=k+1$ more queries suffice. Total $k+2\le 2k+1$.

**Case 2: $f(0)<0$.** Then $r_1r_2r_3>0$, so there are zero or two negative roots. There cannot be zero, since then all three roots would be positive (none is $0$) with sum $0$. So there is one positive root $s$ and two negative roots $t\le u<0$, with $t+u=-s$. Hence $1\le s\le N-1$ and $t\le-\tfrac s2\le u\le -1$, and in fact $s\ge2$.

- For $x\ge0$: $x-t>0$ and $x-u>0$, so the sign of $f(x)$ is the sign of $x-s$. A query at $m\ge 0$ compares $s$ with $m$.
- For an integer $x$ with $-\tfrac s2\le x\le -1$: $x-s<0$ and $x-t\ge0$. If $x-t>0$, the sign of $f(x)$ is minus the sign of $x-u$. If $x=t$, then $t=-\tfrac s2$ forces $u=t=x$ and $f(x)=0$. Either way the answer tells us whether $u<x$, $u=x$, or $u>x$. The candidates for $u$ are $-\lfloor s/2\rfloor,\dots,-1$, i.e. $\lfloor s/2\rfloor$ of them, and $u$ determines $t=-s-u$.

Second move: ask the sign of $f(2^{k+1})$ (note $2^{k+1}=\tfrac23N$).
- *$f(2^{k+1})=0$:* $s=2^{k+1}$, and $u$ has $2^k$ candidates, so $k$ more queries suffice. Total $\le k+2$.
- *$f(2^{k+1})<0$:* $s>2^{k+1}$, so $s\in[2^{k+1}+1,\,3\cdot2^k-1]$, which has $2^k-1$ candidates and needs at most $k-1$ queries. Then $\lfloor s/2\rfloor\le\tfrac{3\cdot2^k-1}{2}<2^{k+1}$, so at most $k$ queries find $u$. Total $\le 2+(k-1)+k=2k+1$.
- *$f(2^{k+1})>0$:* $s\in[2,\,2^{k+1}-1]$, fewer than $2^{k+1}$ candidates, so at most $k$ queries. Then $\lfloor s/2\rfloor\le 2^k-1<2^k$, so at most $k-1$ queries find $u$. Total $\le 2+k+(k-1)=2k+1$.

**Case 3: $f(0)>0$.** Let $g(x)=-f(-x)=x^3+px-q$, whose roots are $-r_1,-r_2,-r_3$. They are again integers with absolute values less than $N$, and the sign of $g(x)$ is minus the sign of $f(-x)$, which Marquis can ask about. Since $g(0)<0$, Marquis runs the Case 2 strategy on $g$, with at most $2k+1$ moves, and recovers the roots of $f$ by negating.

In every case Marquis learns all three roots, hence $f$, within $2k+1$ moves. ∎
